source.title: SAE-Xplainers: Rule-Based Feature Interpretation for Extreme Earth Events
source.authors: Hugo Porta; Emanuele Dalsasso; Chang Xu; Théo Gnassounou; D. Tuia

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether sparse autoencoder features learned from weather and climate model activations can be interpreted by rule-based surrogates, and measures feature absorption. It uses a different setting and method from the toy-network geometry experiments; it does not test their sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE reconstruction/dead-feature metrics, rule-surrogate accuracy, semantic rule statistics, and feature-absorption results. The reconstruction and dead-feature metrics do not establish the geometry or semantic recoverability named by the claim versions, so those rows are recorded under none. Hyperparameter-selection values, cited findings from other work, and downstream-task scores are not recorded as claim rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool on weather/climate transformers (ClimaX, ViT), not LLMs. It assumes SAE features are monosemantic and reports only its own methods' performance: GeoTopK vs TopK reconstruction, and SAE-Xplainer surrogate accuracy and semantics vs neuron and prototype baselines. Feature absorption is used to check the rule interpreters' consistency, shown only on selected example groups and plotted trends. Superposition is invoked as an explanation, never measured. No result measures how features are stored, whether polysemanticity reflects capacity, or whether dictionary features are canonical units.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude that GeoTopK improves reconstruction and feature use, and that SAE-Xplainers faithfully interpret features with literature-consistent rules and can identify absorption. The record's 'sparsity-driven' description of absorption is cited from prior work (Chanin et al.), not shown by this study. Monosemanticity of SAE features is assumed as a hypothesis, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: Unlike the toy-model superposition setup, the paper trains k-sparse SAEs with geographic modulation on the last residual-stream activations of fine-tuned weather/climate encoders, then uses rule-based surrogates. It studies Earth-event data rather than toy networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with dataset, encoder, SAE type, latent dimension/sparsity, rule complexity, and inclusion of spatial context. ClimateNet has weaker rule-surrogate accuracy and higher dead-feature rates; the contribution of spatial context is reported as larger there than for SeasFire.

fits_no_version.finding: Geographic FiLM modulation (GeoTopK) improves SAE reconstruction and lowers dead-feature rates vs TopK on most setups. ViT on SeasFire has lower R2event.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Location-conditioned SAEs reconstruct climate-model activations better, with fewer dead features, than location-agnostic TopK SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: Rule surrogates predict binarized SAE feature activations more accurately than binarized neuron or prototype activations: ~93% vs +22%/+9% gaps on SeasFire, ~85% vs +9%/+5% on ClimateNet. Fire-feature rules match literature drivers more often, with fewer inverse conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In climate transformers, SAE features are more predictable by compact input rules than neurons are, under the study's sampling scheme.

fits_no_version.finding: Rule-similarity grouping surfaces co-occurring SAE feature pairs with nonzero SAEBench absorption scores (0.19, 0.22) in selected examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rule-based surrogates can flag candidate absorbed SAE features in non-language models.

record.problems: The authors state that most runs were done once; uncertainty is reported for the three-run sampling comparison but not for the main SAE and rule-accuracy results. The semantic interpretation analysis is targeted to fire-specific features, and future work is said to need to study rule robustness. The paper does not directly test superposition geometry or causal feature roles.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Hyperparameter-selection values and figure-only points without an explicit textual result were not transcribed as separate outcomes.

untested.parts: No toy model, geometry or sparsity transition.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of other causes of polysemantic neurons.
No LLMs. Spreading of features across neurons is assumed, not measured. SAE recoverability is assumed and only evaluated through the study's own interpreter.

No completeness, stability or canonicality test of SAE features. Absorption is shown only in selected examples used to validate the interpreter. The rule stability in Table 7 concerns surrogate rules, not SAE features.

missing.what: Co-occurrence and absorption score values across rule complexities. Only plotted; no numbers in the text.
missing.versions: none (would matter for V5 only if read as a prevalence)

missing.what: Dead-feature rate and R2 when scaling SAE dimension 4k to 16k for TopK vs GeoTopK

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 support and V5 challenge labels are dropped. The systems are weather/climate ViTs, not LLMs. All quantitative results compare the study's own methods with baselines. Absorption appears only as cherry-picked examples used to validate the interpreter. Most runs are single-seed. The ClimateNet 'superposition across active SAE features' remark is speculation, not a measurement.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy-network experiment or test of overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as competition for capacity, or of dedicated dimensions for important features versus sharing by others.
No test of whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE feature extraction and rule-based prediction of feature activations in weather/climate encoders, not whether LLM activations are spread over many neurons, nor causal feature roles.
Measures feature absorption in selected groups, but does not establish completeness or stability of all dictionary features, or their canonicality across models and training runs.
Uses decoder feature vectors, but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features or test the dimensionality of represented concepts.

rows.value: Authors report that more complex and accurate rules make co-occurrence of features with similar rule conditions more likely.
rows.note: A sparsity-related feature absorption pattern is identified.
rows.check: The trend describes how the absorption-detection scores vary with rule complexity, i.e. the detector's behaviour, not a rate of non-atomic features. No numbers are given in the text.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ClimaX SAE features on SeasFire and ClimateNet; fire-specific GeoTopK features on SeasFire
reader_labels.reason: Rule surrogates predict binarized SAE feature activations with ∼93% and ∼85% accuracy, and many fire-specific feature rules match literature-based drivers (r21–r24, r29).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported accuracy is lower than on SeasFire, and the authors link this partly to a high dead-feature rate and superposition among active features (r22).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Identified absorbed-feature groups in ClimaX GeoTopK on ClimateNet and SeasFire
reader_labels.reason: The study identifies partially absorbed features and reports nonzero absorption scores, indicating that at least some dictionary features are not separate atomic units (r30–r33).
